summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)  
- **Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2226(h) (Adrian's Law)** — the investigating agency shall visually observe the child who is the alleged victim; in a joint investigation DCF and law enforcement shall both observe the child, and DCF policy states that law enforcement's observation does not fulfill DCF's responsibility (DCF PPM 2010)  
- **Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2226(b)** — a joint DCF / law enforcement investigation is mandatory when a report indicates serious physical harm to, serious deterioration of, or sexual abuse of the child and action may be required to protect the child (DCF PPM 1530)

regulations_applicable.title: Agency 30 - KANSAS DEPARTMENT FOR CHILDREN AND FAMILIES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held the father's challenge to the temporary custody order moot because later adjudication and disposition orders superseded it, but retained the appeal under the public-importance exception and upheld K.S.A. 38-2243(f)(3) — the temporary custody standard — against vagueness and overbreadth attack.
key_cases.relevance: The statutory standard authorizing emergency protective custody in Kansas — probable cause that the child's health or welfare may be endangered — survives constitutional challenge.
key_cases.quote: K.S.A. 2011 Supp. 38-2243(f)(3) is neither unconstitutionally vague nor over-broad

key_cases.case_name: Roska ex rel. Roska v. Peterson
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers who entered a family's home and removed a child without a warrant, court order, or exigent circumstances violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, rejecting the argument that the 'special needs' doctrine excuses the warrant requirement for child welfare removals.
key_cases.relevance: Emergency protective custody taken by entering the home without a warrant is lawful in this circuit only if genuine exigent circumstances exist.
key_cases.quote: We find no special need that renders the warrant requirement impracticable when social workers enter a home to remove a child, absent exigent circumstances

key_cases.case_name: Lowther v. Children, Youth & Families Department
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity for an investigator and county defendants on a warrantless-entry claim, holding that under circuit precedent a reasonable official could believe reasonable suspicion of past abuse justified warrantless entry, so the law was not clearly established to the contrary.
key_cases.relevance: It marks the current outer boundary of warrantless entry in the circuit when officials suspect past — not imminent — abuse.
key_cases.quote: a reasonable investigator or officer could reasonably believe warrantless entry was justified by reasonable suspicion of past abuse

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a case beginning with an anonymous hotline call, the court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to the child welfare specialist and the officer who directed a six-year-old's seizure and transport from school for questioning, while reversing as to the officer who merely transported the child and as to the Fourteenth Amendment familial association claim.
key_cases.relevance: Taking custody of a child for investigative purposes short of a true emergency is a seizure subject to Fourth Amendment reasonableness.
key_cases.quote: The district court correctly determined that two of the three defendants were not entitled to qualified immunity on the Fourth Amendment unlawful seizure claim

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children could be taken from him, and that Illinois' presumption of unfitness applied only to unwed fathers denied him equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: State action separating a child from a parent must be accompanied by a hearing on that parent's fitness rather than a categorical presumption.
key_cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

mandatory_reporters: Persons providing medical care or treatment: persons licensed to practice the healing arts, dentistry and optometry, persons in board-approved postgraduate training programs, licensed professional or practical nurses, and chief administrative officers of medical care facilities — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(A)

State-licensed mental health providers: psychologists, masters level psychologists, clinical psychotherapists, social workers, marriage and family therapists, clinical marriage and family therapists, behavioral analysts and assistant behavioral analysts, professional counselors, clinical professional counselors, and registered alcohol and drug abuse counselors — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(B)

Teachers, school administrators and other employees of an educational institution the child attends, and members of the board of directors, employees and officers of the Kansas State High School Activities Association — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(C)

Persons licensed by the secretary of health and environment to provide child care services, and their employees at the place where child care services are provided — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(D)

Firefighters, emergency medical services personnel, law enforcement officers, juvenile intake and assessment workers, court services officers, community corrections officers, and case managers and mediators appointed under Kan. Stat. Ann. §§ 23-3508 and 23-3502 — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(E)

Employees and volunteers of any organization, for profit or not-for-profit, that provides social services to pregnant teenagers, including counseling, adoption services and pregnancy education and maintenance — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(F)
reporting_details: Kansas is not a universal-reporting state: only the professionals listed in Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1) must report, any other person who suspects a child may be a child in need of care may report but is not required to (§ 38-2223(a)(2)), and reports are made to the secretary for children and families — or to the appropriate law enforcement agency when the department is not open for business (§ 38-2223(c)(1)).

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Assignment of the report as designated on the PPS 1002, Initial Assessment (DCF PPM 1500); the 72-hour rule is stated as running from acceptance of the report and excludes weekends and state holidays (DCF PPM 1521)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in DCF PPM 1500 or 1521

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours to initiate an investigation and contact the persons who are the subject of the investigation, then 24 hours from that contact to report the status back to the referring law enforcement agency
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of a law enforcement officer's electronic referral of a child who may be a victim of abuse or neglect
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2231(d)

A later finding is allowed only if a delay is requested by law enforcement, a county or district attorney, the court, or health or mental health professionals, or exceptional circumstances are documented in the case file (DCF PPM 2511 C.). An allowable late finding requires the Child Protection Specialist to enter "Allowable Delay" on the PPS 2011 Case Findings Section IV on or before the case finding due date; if the finding is late for a reason not allowable under PPM 2511 C., the specialist shall document with the finding: "The case finding is delayed due to a non-allowable reason per policy." (DCF PPM 2531 E.)
